title: No. 10 — The Same Subject Continued (The Union as a Safeguard Against Domestic Faction and Insurrection) (Madison)
paragraphs: Among the many advantages a well-constructed Union promises, none deserves to be more carefully developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction. The friend of popular governments never feels more alarm for their character and fate than when he reflects on their tendency toward this dangerous vice. He will not fail, then, to set a fitting value on any plan that, without violating the principles he holds dear, provides a proper cure for it. The instability, injustice, and confusion brought into the public councils have, in truth, been the mortal diseases that have everywhere destroyed popular governments. They remain the favorite and fertile topics from which the enemies of liberty draw their most plausible arguments. The valuable improvements made by the American constitutions on the popular models, both ancient and modern, cannot certainly be too much admired. But it would be unwarranted partiality to claim that they have averted the danger on this side as effectively as we wished and expected. Complaints are heard everywhere from our most thoughtful and virtuous citizens—citizens equally devoted to public and private faith, and to public and personal liberty—that our governments are too unstable, that the public good is ignored in the conflicts of rival parties, and that measures are too often decided not by the rules of justice and the rights of the minority, but by the superior force of an interested and overbearing majority. However much we might wish these complaints had no foundation, the evidence of known facts will not let us deny that they are at least partly true. A candid review of our situation will indeed show that some of the troubles we suffer have been wrongly blamed on the operation of our governments. But it will also show that other causes will not by themselves account for many of our heaviest misfortunes—particularly that prevailing and growing distrust of public commitments and alarm for private rights echoed from one end of the continent to the other. These must be chiefly, if not wholly, the effects of the unsteadiness and injustice with which a factious spirit has tainted our public administrations.

By a faction, I mean a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and driven by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, contrary to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.
There are two ways of curing the harms of faction: one is to remove its causes; the other is to control its effects.

There are again two ways of removing the causes of faction: one is to destroy the liberty essential to its existence; the other is to give every citizen the same opinions, the same passions, and the same interests.

It could never be more truly said than of the first remedy, that it is worse than the disease. Liberty is to faction what air is to fire—a fuel without which it instantly dies. But it would be no less foolish to abolish liberty, which is essential to political life, because it nourishes faction, than to wish to abolish air, which is essential to animal life, because it gives fire its destructive power.

The second expedient is as impractical as the first would be unwise. As long as human reason remains fallible, and people are at liberty to use it, different opinions will be formed. As long as the connection between reason and self-love persists, opinions and passions will influence each other, and the former will become objects to which the latter attach themselves. The diversity in human faculties, from which the rights of property originate, is no less an insurmountable obstacle to a uniformity of interests. The protection of these faculties is the first object of government. From the protection of different and unequal faculties for acquiring property, the possession of different degrees and kinds of property immediately follows. And from the influence of these on the sentiments and views of the respective owners, a division of society into different interests and parties results.

The latent causes of faction are thus sown in human nature; and we see them brought into different degrees of activity everywhere, according to the different circumstances of civil society. A zeal for differing opinions about religion, government, and many other points of speculation as well as practice; an attachment to different leaders ambitiously contending for preeminence and power, or to other persons whose fortunes have stirred human passions—these have, in turn, divided mankind into parties, inflamed them with mutual animosity, and made them much more inclined to vex and oppress each other than to cooperate for their common good. So strong is this human tendency to fall into mutual animosities, that where no substantial occasion presents itself, the most frivolous and fanciful distinctions have been enough to ignite their unfriendly passions and provoke their most violent conflicts. But the most common and lasting source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property. Those who hold property and those who do not have always formed distinct interests in society. Creditors and debtors fall under a similar division. A landed interest, a manufacturing interest, a mercantile interest, a moneyed interest, with many lesser interests, grow up necessarily in civilized nations and divide them into different classes driven by different sentiments and views. The regulation of these various and clashing interests is the principal task of modern legislation, and weaves the spirit of party and faction into the necessary and ordinary operations of government.

No man is allowed to be a judge in his own cause, because his interest would certainly bias his judgment and quite likely corrupt his integrity. With equal—indeed greater—reason, a body of men is unfit to be both judges and parties at the same time. Yet what are many of the most important acts of legislation but so many judicial determinations—not, indeed, concerning the rights of single persons, but concerning the rights of large bodies of citizens? And what are the different classes of legislators but advocates and parties to the causes they decide? Is a law proposed concerning private debts? It is a question on which creditors are parties on one side and debtors on the other. Justice ought to hold the balance between them. Yet the parties are, and must be, the judges themselves; and the most numerous party, or in other words the most powerful faction, must be expected to prevail. Should domestic manufactures be encouraged, and to what degree, by restrictions on foreign manufactures? These are questions that would be decided differently by the landed and the manufacturing classes—and probably by neither with sole regard to justice and the public good. The apportionment of taxes on the various kinds of property is an act that seems to require the most exact impartiality; yet there is perhaps no legislative act in which a dominant party has greater opportunity and temptation to trample the rules of justice. Every shilling with which they overburden the smaller number is a shilling saved to their own pockets.

It is useless to say that enlightened statesmen will be able to adjust these clashing interests and make them all serve the public good. Enlightened statesmen will not always be at the helm. Nor, in many cases, can such an adjustment be made at all without taking into account indirect and remote considerations, which will rarely outweigh the immediate interest one party may find in disregarding the rights of another or the good of the whole.
The conclusion to which we are brought is that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be found in the means of controlling its EFFECTS.

If a faction consists of less than a majority, relief is supplied by the republican principle, which enables the majority to defeat its sinister aims by regular vote. It may clog the administration, it may convulse society; but it will be unable to carry out its violence and conceal it under the forms of the Constitution. When a majority is included in a faction, however, the form of popular government enables it to sacrifice the public good and the rights of other citizens to its ruling passion or interest. To secure the public good and private rights against the danger of such a faction, and at the same time to preserve the spirit and form of popular government, is therefore the great object to which our inquiries are directed. Let me add that it is the great desideratum by which this form of government can be rescued from the disgrace it has so long suffered, and recommended to the esteem and adoption of mankind.

By what means is this object attainable? Plainly, by one of only two. Either the existence of the same passion or interest in a majority at the same time must be prevented; or the majority, having such a coexisting passion or interest, must be made—by their number and local situation—unable to coordinate and carry out schemes of oppression. If the impulse and the opportunity are allowed to coincide, we know well that neither moral nor religious motives can be relied on as adequate controls. They are not found to be such on the injustice and violence of individuals, and they lose their effectiveness in proportion to the number combined together—that is, in proportion as their effectiveness becomes most needed.

From this view of the subject, we may conclude that a pure democracy—by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens who assemble and administer the government in person—can admit of no cure for the harms of faction. A common passion or interest will, in almost every case, be felt by a majority of the whole. Communication and concert result from the form of government itself; and there is nothing to check the temptation to sacrifice the weaker party or an unpopular individual. Hence such democracies have always been spectacles of turbulence and contention; have always been found incompatible with personal security or the rights of property; and have generally been as short in life as they have been violent in death. Theoretical politicians who have championed this kind of government have wrongly supposed that by reducing mankind to perfect equality in political rights, they would also be perfectly equalized and assimilated in their possessions, opinions, and passions.

A republic—by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place—opens a different prospect and promises the cure we are seeking. Let us examine the points in which it differs from pure democracy, and we shall understand both the nature of the cure and the effectiveness it must derive from the Union.

The two great points of difference between a democracy and a republic are: first, in a republic the government is delegated to a small number of citizens elected by the rest; second, the greater number of citizens and the greater extent of territory over which a republic may be extended.

The effect of the first difference is, on one hand, to refine and enlarge the public views by passing them through the medium of a chosen body of citizens, whose wisdom may best discern the true interest of their country, and whose patriotism and love of justice will be least likely to sacrifice it to temporary or partial considerations. Under such an arrangement, it may well happen that the public voice, expressed by the representatives of the people, will be more consonant with the public good than if expressed by the people themselves, gathered for the purpose. On the other hand, the effect may be reversed. Men of factious tempers, local prejudices, or sinister designs may—by intrigue, corruption, or other means—first obtain the votes and then betray the interests of the people. The question is whether small or extensive republics are more favorable to the election of proper guardians of the public welfare; and it is clearly decided in favor of the latter by two obvious considerations:

First, however small the republic may be, the representatives must be raised to a certain number to guard against the cabals of a few. And however large it may be, they must be limited to a certain number to guard against the confusion of a multitude. Hence the number of representatives in the two cases is not proportional to the number of constituents, and is proportionally greater in the small republic. It follows that if the proportion of fit characters is no smaller in the large republic than in the small one, the large republic will present a greater range of choice and therefore a greater probability of a fit selection.

Second, since each representative in the large republic will be chosen by a greater number of citizens than in the small one, it will be harder for unworthy candidates to practice successfully the vicious arts by which elections are too often won. And the votes of the people, being freer, will be more likely to settle on men possessing the most attractive merit and the most widespread and established characters.

It must be admitted that in this, as in most other cases, there is a middle ground, on either side of which inconveniences lie. By enlarging the number of electors too much, you render the representatives too little acquainted with all their local circumstances and lesser interests; by reducing it too much, you render him too attached to these and too little fit to grasp and pursue great and national objects. The federal Constitution forms a happy combination in this respect: the great and aggregate interests are referred to the national legislature, the local and particular to the State legislatures.

The other point of difference is the greater number of citizens and extent of territory that can be brought within the compass of republican government than of democratic government. And it is this circumstance chiefly that makes factious combinations less to be feared in a republic than in a democracy. The smaller the society, the fewer the distinct parties and interests composing it; the fewer the distinct parties and interests, the more frequently will a majority be found of the same party; and the smaller the number of individuals composing a majority, and the smaller the area in which they are placed, the more easily will they coordinate and carry out their plans of oppression. Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will share a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens; or if such a common motive exists, it will be harder for all who feel it to discover their own strength and to act together. Besides other obstacles, where there is awareness of unjust or dishonorable purposes, communication is always checked by distrust in proportion to the number whose agreement is needed.

Hence it clearly appears that the same advantage which a republic has over a democracy in controlling the effects of faction is enjoyed by a large republic over a small one—is enjoyed by the Union over the States composing it. Does the advantage consist in the substitution of representatives whose enlightened views and virtuous sentiments raise them above local prejudices and schemes of injustice? It will not be denied that the representation of the Union is most likely to possess these necessary qualities. Does it consist in the greater security afforded by a greater variety of parties against any one party being able to outnumber and oppress the rest? To an equal degree, the increased variety of parties contained within the Union increases this security. Does it, finally, consist in the greater obstacles set against the concert and success of the secret wishes of an unjust and interested majority? Here too, the extent of the Union gives it the most obvious advantage.

The influence of factious leaders may kindle a flame within their own States, but will be unable to spread a general conflagration through the other States. A religious sect may degenerate into a political faction in part of the Confederacy; but the variety of sects scattered over its entire surface must secure the national councils against any danger from that source. A rage for paper money, for the abolition of debts, for an equal division of property, or for any other improper or wicked project, will be less likely to pervade the whole body of the Union than a particular member of it—in the same proportion as such a disease is more likely to taint a particular county or district than an entire State.

In the extent and proper structure of the Union, therefore, we see a republican remedy for the diseases most natural to republican government. And the degree of pleasure and pride we feel in being republicans should match our zeal in cherishing the spirit and supporting the character of Federalists.
